name: Treks and trails
tagline: Teahouse to teahouse, village to pass
summary: Nepal's trails were roads long before they were treks: salt, rice and wool moved on them for centuries. We plan teahouse treks from three-day ridge walks to three-week circuits, with licensed guides, honest grading and rest days placed where the altitude asks for them.
intro: Most of Nepal's hill and mountain villages are still linked by footpaths, and the teahouses that line them grew out of homes that fed traders. A trek here is less a wilderness trip than a walk through lived-in country, where you sleep in family lodges and eat what the kitchen cooks that day.

We grade every route by hours walked, height gained and the highest night's sleep, not by adjectives. Since April 2023, foreign trekkers in most national parks and conservation areas must walk with a licensed guide: check current status before you travel.

name: High altitude
tagline: Above 3,000 m, with time to adjust
summary: Everest, Annapurna Base Camp, Upper Mustang, Gokyo, Manaslu and Kanchenjunga. Routes built on the 'climb high, sleep low' rule, with rest days at Namche, Manang and Dingboche-type stops, because acclimatisation decides how the trip feels.
intro: Above about 3,000 m the body needs time. The usual guide is to raise your sleeping height by no more than 300–500 m a day once you are above 3,000 m, and to take a rest day for every 1,000 m or so gained.

Our itineraries follow that rule and show the sleeping height of every night. If you have heart or lung conditions, speak to your doctor before booking, and hold insurance that covers helicopter evacuation to the highest point on your route.

name: Heritage and temples
tagline: Durbar squares, stupas and old towns
summary: The Kathmandu Valley alone holds seven monument zones inscribed together as one UNESCO World Heritage Site. Add Lumbini, Tansen, Gorkha, Nuwakot, Janakpur and Lo Manthang, and you can read Nepal's history in brick, wood and stone.
intro: Nepal's old towns are not museums. People still worship at the temples, draw water from the stone spouts and hold feasts in the courtyards their guthi trusts have kept for centuries.
We plan heritage days around those living hours: the morning puja, the evening bhajan, the festival chariot. Our guides know which courtyards welcome visitors and which ask for quiet.

name: Wildlife and jungle
tagline: Rhino, tiger, gharial and river dolphin
summary: Chitwan, Bardia, Shuklaphanta, Parsa and Koshi Tappu: the Terai parks where Nepal's greater one-horned rhinoceros and Bengal tiger numbers have risen. Jeep drives, canoe trips and walking safaris with naturalists, matched to the season.
intro: The Terai's parks run on seasons. Tall elephant grass is cut and burned in late winter, which opens the view from February to May, while the monsoon closes many tracks from June to September.
We pair each park with a lodge whose naturalists we trust and plan at least three activities a day. We do not book elephant rides; we explain why on our Chitwan guide pages.

name: Spiritual and pilgrimage
tagline: Lumbini, Pashupatinath, Muktinath and the gompas
summary: The Buddha's birthplace at Lumbini, Shiva's temple at Pashupatinath, Muktinath sacred to Hindus and Buddhists alike, Gosaikunda's high lake, Janakpur's Janaki Mandir and the monasteries of Khumbu and Mustang.
intro: In Nepal, Hindu and Buddhist practice often share the same ground. Swayambhu has Hindu shrines in its courtyard; Muktinath's 108 spouts are walked by sadhus and Tibetan Buddhist pilgrims on the same morning.

We time visits to ritual hours and brief you on dress and photography rules for each site. Several pilgrimages follow the lunar calendar, so dates move each year: check current status before you travel.

name: Food and festivals
tagline: Feasts, markets and the lunar calendar
summary: Newar samay baji and yomari, Thakali dal bhat, Sherpa shyakpa, Tharu ghonghi, Mithila sweets, Ilam's tea and tongba in the eastern hills. And the festivals that bring them out: Dashain, Tihar, Indra Jatra, Bisket, Tiji and Chhath.
intro: Food in Nepal changes with height as much as with region. Rice gives way to millet, buckwheat and barley as the trail climbs, and every community has a feast dish tied to a festival.
Most festivals follow the lunar calendar or the Bikram Sambat year, which began its year 2083 in April 2026. We confirm each date before we build the route.

name: Villages and homestays
tagline: Sleep in a family home, eat at their table
summary: Community homestays in Tharu, Gurung, Magar and Tamang villages, from Barauli and Amaltari in the Terai to Ghandruk, Sirubari-style hill villages, Gatlang and Briddim on the Tamang Heritage Trail.
intro: Nepal's community homestay programmes let villages host travellers in family homes, with income shared through a local committee. Rooms are simple and clean; the welcome, the food and the evening dances are the point.
We choose homestays run by community committees, brief you on customs before you arrive, and pay hosts directly for the nights you stay.

name: Lakes and rivers
tagline: Phewa, Rara, Gosaikunda and the snow-fed rivers
summary: Rowing boats on Phewa and Begnas, Rara's blue water in the far west, the sacred lakes of Gosaikunda and Gokyo, rafting on the Trishuli, Seti and Karnali, and the river confluences where Nepalis bathe on festival days.
intro: Nepal's rivers start in Tibet or on its own glaciers and cut south through the hills in deep gorges, which makes for strong rafting and holy confluences called triveni or dovan.
Rafting runs are graded by season: some are gentle in spring and serious in autumn when water is high. We match the river to your experience and the month.

name: Family trips
tagline: Short drives, short walks, big views
summary: Routes with drives under five hours, walks children can finish, jungle days in Chitwan, boating in Pokhara and a short trek such as Poon Hill or Dhampus that ends at a lodge with hot water.
intro: Families travel better with fewer hotel changes and shorter days. We cap most road days, choose lodges with space and plan activities with a clear start and end.
High routes are harder on children, who may not report altitude symptoms clearly. We usually keep families below 3,000 m and explain why before you book.

name: Honeymoons
summary: A lake-view lodge in Pokhara, a heritage courtyard hotel in Kathmandu, a jungle lodge in Chitwan and a sunrise above the clouds at Nagarkot or Dhulikhel. Fewer moves, longer stays.
intro: A good honeymoon route moves less than a sightseeing tour. We build around three or four bases, with two nights as the minimum anywhere.
We add a few occasions: a dawn flight past Everest, a private boat on Phewa, a dinner in a Newar courtyard. The rest of the time is yours.

name: Photography
tagline: Light, height and the right hour
summary: Autumn's clear air, spring rhododendrons, festival chariots, the walled city of Lo Manthang and the mountain views at Poon Hill, Kala Patthar and Gokyo Ri, timed for the light.
intro: Nepal's best mountain light usually comes in October and November, when the monsoon has washed the air. Spring brings haze but also rhododendron forests in flower.
We plan photo routes around sunrise and sunset times and festival processions, and we brief you on where photography is not welcome, such as some shrines and cremation ghats.

name: Adventure sports
summary: Tandem paragliding from Sarangkot, rafting on the Trishuli and Karnali, the Bhote Koshi bungee, zip-lining above Pokhara, mountain biking in the valley rim and trekking peaks such as Island Peak.
intro: Pokhara is one of the busiest paragliding sites in Asia, and Nepal's snow-fed rivers give multi-day rafting that few countries can match.
We book operators we know and build in weather days. Adventure activities need specific insurance cover: check your policy before you travel.

name: Crafts and makers
summary: Bhaktapur's potters, Patan's lost-wax metal casters, Bungamati's woodcarvers, lokta paper makers, Palpa's Dhaka weavers, Chainpur's brass workers and Mithila painters in Janakpur.
intro: Many of Nepal's crafts are still family trades passed down in the same streets. Patan's bronze casting and Bhaktapur's woodcarving supplied temples across the Himalaya.
We arrange studio visits where you can watch and try, and we take no commission on anything you buy.

name: Slow and wellness
summary: Meditation courses in Lumbini's monastic zone and the Kathmandu Valley, yoga retreats near Pokhara, monastery stays, and slow days in Bandipur, Tansen or a farm in Nuwakot.
intro: Nepal has a long tradition of retreat, from Buddhist meditation centres around Kathmandu and Lumbini to Hindu ashrams.
We build slow routes with two or three long stays rather than many short ones, and we tell you plainly which retreats are silent, which are residential, and which suit a first-timer.
